fixed.before: XXV. In Gaul the disease often mentioned invaded the province of Marseille, and a severe famine oppressed the people of Angers, Nantes and Le Mans. For these are the beginnings of sorrows, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “There will be pestilences and famines and earthquakes in various places” (Matt. 24:7); “and false christs and false prophets will arise” (ibid. 24:11); “and they will give signs and wonders in the sky, so as to lead the elect into error” (Mark 13:22). And so it happened at the present time. A certain man from Bourges, as he himself afterwards confessed, had gone into the forest glades and was cutting wood to meet the needs of some work, when a swarm of flies surrounded him; for this reason he was held to be out of his mind for two years. From this one may understand that it was a wickedness sent by the devil. After this he passed through the neighbouring cities and went to the province of Arles, and there, dressed in skins, he prayed as if he were a man of religion; and to make sport of him, the Adversary gave him the power of divination. Then, to advance in greater wickedness, he moved from that place, left the said province, and entered the territory of the Gévaudan, proclaiming himself someone great and not afraid to profess himself Christ, taking with him a certain woman as his sister, whom he had called Mary. A multitude of people flocked to him, bringing the sick, whom he touched and restored to health. Those who came to him brought him gold and silver and clothing. He gave these away to the poor, the more easily to lead them astray, prostrating himself on the ground and pouring out prayer with the woman mentioned; and rising again, he ordered those standing around to worship him. He foretold the future, and announced that sickness would come to some, losses to others, and to a few well-being to come. But all this he did by devilish arts and by I know not what illusions. An immense multitude of people was led astray by him, and not only the simpler country folk but even priests of the Church. More than three thousand people followed him. Meanwhile he began to rob and plunder some whom he met on the road; the spoils, however, he gave away to those who had nothing. He threatened bishops and citizens with death because they disdained to worship him. Entering the territory of the city of Velay, he came to the place they call Anicium; and he halted with his whole army at the nearby basilicas, drawing up a battle line to make war on Aurelius, who was then bishop there, and sending messengers ahead of him, men with naked bodies, dancing and capering, to announce his coming. The bishop, astonished at this, sent capable men to him to ask what these doings of his meant. When one of them, the senior, had bowed down as if to kiss his knees and to bar his way, [the impostor] ordered him to be seized and stripped; at once that man drew his sword and cut him to pieces, and that Christ, who ought rather to be called Antichrist, fell and died, and all who were with him were scattered. That Mary, handed over to torture, all his phantasms [...]; [those] whom he had thrown into confusion by devilish deceit so that they believed [in him] never returned to a sound mind, but always professed that he was, as it were, Christ, and that that Mary had a share in the godhead. Throughout all Gaul, too, many arose who by these tricks attached to themselves certain foolish women, who in their frenzy would proclaim them saints, and so set themselves up as great among the people; we have seen many of them, and have tried by rebuking them to call them back from their error.

fixed.before: In the second year of King Childebert, when Merovech saw his father intent on this plan, he thought of going to Brunhild, taking Duke Guntram with him, and said: “God forbid that the basilica of the lord Martin should suffer violence on my account, or that his region should be brought into captivity through me.” And entering the basilica while he was keeping vigil, he presented at the tomb of the blessed Martin the things he had with him, praying that the saint would come to his aid and grant him his favour, so that he might receive the kingdom. At that time Count Leudast, who was laying many traps for him out of love for Fredegund, at last caught by trickery his servants who had gone out into the countryside and put them to the sword, and he wanted to kill [Merovech] himself, if he could find him in a suitable place. But [Merovech], following Guntram's advice and wishing to avenge himself, ordered Marileif the chief physician to be seized as he was returning from the king's presence; and having had him beaten very severely, and his gold and silver and the other things he was carrying taken from him, he left him naked. And he would certainly have killed him, had [Marileif] not slipped out of the hands of those beating him and fled to the church; afterwards we clothed him, obtained his life, and sent him back to Poitiers. Merovech spoke of many crimes of his father and stepmother; and although these were partly true, I believe it was not pleasing to God that they should be made public by a son, as I learned from what followed. For one day, when I had been invited to his table and we were sitting together, he humbly asked that something be read for the instruction of the soul. I opened the book of Solomon and seized on the first verse that met me, which said: “The eye that looks against a father, may the ravens of the valleys dig it out” (Prov. 30:17). He did not understand, but I considered that this verse had been prepared by the Lord. Then Guntram sent a servant to a certain woman, known to him since the time of King Charibert, who had a spirit of python, so that she might tell him what was going to happen. He claimed, moreover, that before this time she had foretold to him not only the year but also the day and the hour in which King Charibert would die. She sent back to him by the servants this message: “It shall be that King Chilperic dies this year, and that King Merovech, shutting out his brothers, takes the whole kingdom. And you will hold the dukedom of his whole kingdom for five years. In the sixth year, in one of the cities that lie on the bed of the Loire, on its right side, you will obtain the grace of a bishopric with the favour of the people, and old and full of days you will depart from this world.” When the servants returned and reported this to their master, he was at once puffed up with vanity, as if he were already sitting on the throne of the church of Tours, and he brought these words to me. Laughing at his folly, I said: “These things must be asked of God; for what the devil promises ought not to be believed. He is a liar from the beginning, and has never stood in the truth” (John 8:44). And when he went away abashed, I laughed heartily at the man who thought such things could be believed. Then one night, after the vigils had been celebrated in the basilica of the holy bishop, as I lay on my bed and had fallen asleep, I saw an angel flying through the air. As he passed over the holy basilica, he said in a loud voice: “Alas, alas! God has struck Chilperic and all his sons; and none of those who came forth from his loins will survive to rule his kingdom for ever.” At that time he had four sons by different wives, not counting daughters. When these things were later fulfilled, then I knew clearly that what the soothsayers had promised was false. While these men were staying at the basilica of Saint Martin, Queen Fredegund sent to Guntram Boso (she was already secretly protecting him on account of Theudebert's death), saying: “If you can drive Merovech out of the basilica so that he may be killed, you will receive a great reward from me.” He, thinking the killers were ready at hand, said to Merovech: “Why do we sit here like sluggards and cowards, and hide like dullards round this basilica? Let our horses be brought, and let us take hawks and exercise ourselves in hunting with hounds, and enjoy the open views.” He did this cunningly, to separate him from the holy basilica. Guntram was otherwise a good man; but he was all too ready for perjury, and indeed he never swore an oath to any of his friends that he did not promptly break. So they went out of the basilica, as we said, and went on to the house at Jocundiacum near the city; but Merovech was harmed by no one. And since Guntram was then being accused, as we said, of Theudebert's death, King Chilperic sent messengers with a written letter to the tomb of Saint Martin, which contained the request that the blessed Martin should write back to him whether or not it was lawful to drag Guntram out of his basilica. But the deacon Baudegil, who delivered this letter, placed a blank sheet on the holy tomb together with the one he had brought. And when he had waited three days and received no reply, he went back to Chilperic. Chilperic then sent others to exact oaths from Guntram that he would not leave the basilica without his knowledge. Guntram swore eagerly and gave the altar cloth as his surety that he would never go out from there without the king's order. Merovech, not believing the prophetess, laid three books on the saint's tomb, namely the Psalter, Kings and the Gospels; and keeping vigil all night, he asked the blessed confessor to show him what would happen, and whether he could receive the kingdom or not, so that he might learn it from the Lord's revealing. After this, having continued three days in fasting, vigils and prayers, he went to the blessed tomb again and opened the book, which was Kings; and the first verse of the page he opened was this: “Because you have forsaken the Lord your God and walked after strange gods, and have not done what is right in his sight, therefore the Lord your God has delivered you into the hands of your enemies” (3 Kings 9:9). In the Psalter this verse was found: “Yet because of deceitfulness you have set evils for them; you cast them down while they were being lifted up. How have they come to desolation? Suddenly they have failed; they have perished because of their iniquities” (Ps. 71:18–19). And in the Gospels this was found: “You know that after two days the Passover will come, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified” (Matt. 26:2). Confounded by these answers, he wept for a very long time at the tomb of the blessed bishop, and then, taking Duke Guntram with him, departed with five hundred men or more. Having left the holy basilica, while he was travelling through the territory of Auxerre, he was captured by Erpo, a duke of King Guntram. And while he was being held by him, he slipped away by some chance I do not know, and entered the basilica of Saint Germanus. When King Guntram heard this, he was moved to anger, fined Erpo seven hundred gold pieces and removed him from his office, saying: “You have held, as my brother says, his enemy. If you meant to do this, you ought first to have brought him to me; but if not, you ought not even to have touched a man you were only pretending to hold.” King Chilperic's army advanced as far as Tours, plundered that region, burned it and laid it waste; nor did it spare the property of Saint Martin, but whatever it laid hands on it carried off, without any regard for God or fear of him. Merovech, having stayed nearly two months at the aforesaid basilica, took flight and made his way as far as Queen Brunhild; but he was not received by the Austrasians. His father moved an army against the people of Champagne, thinking he was hidden there; but he did no harm, and could not find him.

fixed.before: Preface. Having undertaken to write on the character and power of simple drugs, in the first two books we chose to expose the faulty methods of argument by which most of the more recent physicians go very greatly astray. In the third we made a kind of elementary introduction to the whole teaching; then next, in the fourth, we inquired into the nature of flavours, striving to discover everything that it is possible to gain from them towards the knowledge of the powers. At the end of that book we also discussed the qualities in simple drugs that relate to smell. In the fifth, passing on to the remaining class of powers, which takes its name from the effects they naturally produce, there too we demonstrated the nature and substance of each. All the general accounts of the power of simples, then, seem now to be complete; it is time to move on to the particular ones, or those by species, or however one may wish to name them. These would be worked out for each drug separately, as we also did right at the start, examining water and vinegar in the first of these treatises and oil and rose oil in the second; except that there our discussion proceeded by way of examples, against those who had pronounced incorrectly about their power, whereas here I shall go through each briefly, no longer concerned whether anyone has pronounced badly about any of them, but writing what seems to me most true, without controversy against those who are mistaken. That the account will not only be unclear to those who forget what came before, but will also lack the credibility of demonstration, is clear, I think, even if I do not say it; but it is perhaps better that I too should remind [the reader], first, that the test of the power of drugs must be made on the best-tempered constitution, and next, on simple diseases. And if anyone should wish to draw inferences by way of indication about the power itself from the qualities of taste as well, we showed the method for these too in the fourth [book]. So if anyone, having read the earlier books carelessly, or not having read them at all, comes straight to this book, in a hurry to gain knowledge of the power of drugs as quickly as possible, he will not have a secure knowledge of them. Since of all drugs some are parts of animals or plants or fruits, or certain saps or juices of these, while others are taken from mines, it seemed better to me to go through plants first, because their class is both the largest and the strongest in power, then next to speak of the mined substances, and then in this way to come to the parts of animals. And indeed I decided that the order of writing about them should also be made by letters, writing first about those plants whose names begin with the letter alpha, second those that begin with beta, and so on to the third, fourth, fifth and all the rest in succession according to the order of the letters. This is how Pamphilus too composed his treatise on herbs. But he turned aside into certain old wives' tales and some silly Egyptian sorceries, together with certain incantations which people pronounce over the herbs as they gather them. And indeed he has used [them] for amulets and other trickeries which are not only idle curiosities, nor merely outside the art of medicine, but are also all false. We, however, shall mention none of these things, nor, further, their silly metamorphoses. For we do not suppose such tales to be useful even to very small children, let alone to those eager to pursue the works of medicine. And it seems to me that 'life is short, the art long' was said by Hippocrates right at the beginning of the Aphorisms so that we should not use up our time on useless things, but should hasten, as far as we can, to take the shortest route through the most useful parts of the art themselves. Moreover, it seemed to me superfluous to add here these many Egyptian and Babylonian names of the herbs, and all those that some people have given them privately or symbolically. For it is better, if anyone wishes to busy himself with these too, to read on his own and by himself the books of the *Antiphrazontes* [substitute-namers]. For that is how those who compile them title them, as Xenocrates of Aphrodisias also did, a man in other respects much given to curious lore and not free of sorcery. As for Pamphilus, who composed the work on herbs, it is plain from what he writes himself that he is a grammarian who has neither seen the herbs he describes nor tested their power, but has trusted all who wrote before him without scrutiny. He copied out books, pointlessly adding a mass of names for each herb, then next relating whether any of them had been transformed from a human being, then adding incantations and certain libations and fumigations for taking them up out of the earth, and other silly sorceries of that kind. But Dioscorides of Anazarbus wrote in five books on the material useful for everything, recording not only herbs but also trees, fruits, juices and saps, and further all the mined substances and the parts of animals. And he seems to me to have produced the most complete treatise of all on the material of drugs. For much was well written about them by earlier writers too, but by no one in this way about all of them, unless one were to praise Tanitros, the [follower] of Asclepiades; for by him too other things are said well, except for his reasonings about causes. Whoever wishes to become experienced in materia medica should read these, and in addition the works of Heraclides of Tarentum, Crateuas and Mantias. But these men did not write in the same way, nor is everything gathered into one, as with Dioscorides, who titled his five books *On Material*; rather they wrote separately, as it happened, on the preparation and testing of drugs, as Heraclides of Tarentum did, and separately on purgation, or preliminary draughts, or clysters, as Mantias did; and separately on easily obtained remedies, like Apollonius, or on remedies by [bodily] region, like Mantias. Most of the use of drugs, however, has been written up in the therapeutic treatises themselves, both by the ancients and also by nearly all the more recent writers; for much was said by Hippocrates, and by Euryphon, Dieuches, Diocles, Pleistonicus, Praxagoras and Herophilus, and there is no ancient man who did not contribute something to the art, more or less, towards the knowledge of drugs, without the sorcery and imposture that Andreas later displayed; so that whoever has leisure to spend time with useful books written about drugs has many from the ancients, as has been said, and not a few from the more recent writers, down to the circle of Pamphilus and Archigenes. Moreover, Rufus of Ephesus also wrote of many drugs in his therapeutic books, and four [books] on herbs in hexameter verse were composed by him; and there is no fear of useful books running out, even if someone wishes to read nothing else all his life but [books] about drugs. One should, however, keep away from Andreas and those who are similar impostors, and much more still from Pamphilus, who has never seen, even in a dream, the herbs whose forms he attempts to describe. For people of this kind, as indeed Heraclides of Tarentum likened them, are most like the criers who announce the marks of appearance of a runaway slave without ever having seen him themselves. For they get the marks from those who know, and recite them like an incantation, though they could not recognise them even if the man being cried happened to be standing beside them. For my part, I used to find fault with those who first wrote descriptions of the forms of herbs, thinking it better for the learner to become an eyewitness at the side of the teacher himself, and not to become like the helmsmen [who learn] from a book. For in this way the teaching would be carried out more truly and more clearly by teachers, not of herbs only, or shrubs or trees, but of all other drugs as well. But if one does after all need a book, who is so wretched as to pass over those of Dioscorides, Niger, Heraclides, Crateuas and countless others who grew old in the art, and put up with the grammarian's books of a man writing incantations and metamorphoses and the sacred herbs of decans and demons? That sorcerers, men who have made it their business to astound the great crowd, put such things together, you can learn from the books of Pamphilus themselves, who first wrote up among the herbs southernwood, which happens to be familiar to all of us, then next the chaste tree, this too a quite familiar shrub, then *agrōstis* [couch grass], a plant not unknown even to laymen, then alkanet, of which no one is ignorant either, as indeed no one is of maidenhair, written next after it. In these, then, he writes nothing beyond what we know; but after these he mentions a herb called, as he says himself, 'eagle', about which he admits that none of the Greeks has said anything, but that it is written in one of the books attributed to Hermes the Egyptian, which contains the thirty-six sacred herbs of the horoscopes; these are all plainly nonsense and fictions of the compiler, very like the *Ophionika* ['Snake-Victories'] of Konchlas. For there never was any Konchlas at all; the name was put together as a joke, as was everything else written in his book. And these thirty-six herbs go no further than their names, with no real thing underlying them. But Pamphilus, like many others, perhaps had leisure to write useless tales into books; we, even now, consider that we are wasting our time by mentioning them any further. Let us begin, then, at once on the useful things.

fixed.before: Then next he takes up again the account of the seven ruling *daimones* [spirit-beings], who are in no way named by Christians but are, I think, accepted by the Ophites. And indeed, in the diagram that we too acquired on their account, we found the order set out in the same way as Celsus set it out. Celsus, then, said that the first was formed in the shape of a lion, without stating what those truly most impious people call him; but we found that the angel of the Creator who is praised in the holy scriptures, this one that foul diagram said was Michael, the lion-shaped. Again, Celsus said that the next, the second, is a bull; but the diagram that we had said that the bull-shaped one was Suriel. Then Celsus [said that] the third [was] some amphibious creature, hissing horribly; but the diagram said that the third was Raphael, serpent-shaped. Again, Celsus said that the fourth had the form of an eagle; but the diagram said that the eagle-shaped one was Gabriel. Then Celsus said that the fifth had the face of a bear; but the diagram said that the bear-shaped one was Thauthabaoth. Then Celsus said that the sixth is reported among them to have the face of a dog; but the diagram said that he was Erathaoth. Then Celsus said that the seventh had the face of an ass and was named Thaphabaoth or Onoel; but we found in the diagram that this one is called Onoel or Thartharaoth, being somewhat ass-shaped. We too decided to set out such things exactly, so that we may not seem ignorant of what Celsus professed to know, but may also show that we Christians know them more exactly than he does, as the doctrines not of Christians but of people wholly alien to salvation, who in no way enrol themselves under Jesus, or a Saviour, or God, or a Teacher, or the Son of God.

fixed.before: As for what you put forward, that it is by no means to be dismissed that there are producers of effective images, I would be amazed if any of the *theourgoi* [practitioners of *theourgia*, ritual "god-work"] who contemplate the true forms of the gods would accept it. For why would anyone take images in exchange for what truly is, and be carried down from the very first things to the last? Or do we not know that in such shadow-painting everything is faint, and that these are not true appearances of the true, and that the goods appear as seeming, but never as being? And the other [features] likewise come in, borne along in becoming, but they possess nothing genuine, nothing perfect, nothing clear. The manner of their making shows it too. For their maker is not a god but a man; nor are they brought forth from uniform and intelligible essences, but from the matter that is taken [for them]. What good, then, could come from what sprouts out of matter and from the material and corporeal powers about matter and in bodies? Or from what is constituted by human art, being weaker even than the very humans who give it its being? And by what kind of art is this image fashioned? It is said: by the demiurgic [art]. But that [art] was productive of true essences, not of some images; so that the image-making art is many removes from the generative creation of true things. Nor does it preserve any analogy to divine making: for it is not through the natural motions of the heavens, or through partial matter, or through powers divided in this way, that God creates all things; but by thoughts and wills and immaterial forms, through the eternal and supercosmic and encosmic *psychē* [soul], he creates the worlds. The maker of images, though, is said to produce them through the stars that revolve.

fixed.before: And how [do] sorceries [work]? By sympathy, and by there being by nature a concord of like things and an opposition of unlike things, and by the variety of the many powers that contribute to one living being. For even when no one else contrives anything, many things are drawn and bewitched; and the true magic is the Love in the All, and again the Strife. And this is the first sorcerer and potion-maker, and people, having observed him, use his potions and spells on one another. For because it is natural to love, and the things that produce love draw towards one another, an art of erotic drawing through sorcery has arisen, of people who apply by contact different natures to different people, natures that draw together and have love lying within them; and they join one *psychē* [soul] to another, as if they were tying together plants set apart from each other. They also make use of figures that have powers, and by putting themselves into such-and-such postures they silently draw powers onto themselves, being within one [whole and acting] upon one. fixed.before: The temple of Serapis at Alexandria has, I think, been heard of by everyone, and is actually known to most. The site is raised on high not by nature but by hand and construction, up a hundred steps or more, and extends on every side in vast square spaces; and everything, up to where one comes out at the topmost floor, is built of vaulted work, which, with huge light-openings from above and hidden inner chambers divided off from one another, served the use of various ministries and secret rites. Further, in the upper parts the outermost spaces of the whole circuit are taken up by halls and *pastophoria* (chambers), and by buildings rising to a height, in which the temple-keepers used to live, or those whom they called *hagneuontes*, that is, those who keep themselves chaste. Behind these, too, colonnades set out in square rows ran round the whole circuit on the inside. In the middle of the whole space stood the shrine, raised on precious columns and built on the outside, amply and magnificently, of marble. In it the image of Serapis was so huge that with its right hand it touched one wall and with its left the other: a monster said to have been made of every kind of metal and wood. The inner walls of the sanctuary were held to be clad first with plates of gold, over these with silver, and last with bronze, to serve as protection for the more precious metals. There were also certain things contrived by trickery and art for the astonishment and wonder of the beholders. A very small window on the side of the sunrise was so fitted that, on the day on which it had been ordained that the image of the Sun be carried in to greet Serapis, the timing having been carefully observed, as the image entered, a ray of the sun directed through that window lit up the mouth and lips of Serapis, so that, as the people looked on, Serapis seemed to be greeted with a kiss by the Sun. There was another kind of fraud too, of this sort. The nature of the magnet stone is said to have this power, that it snatches and draws iron to itself. An image of the Sun had been made by a craftsman's hand of the finest iron for this very purpose: that the stone, whose nature, as we said, is to draw iron to itself, being fixed above in the panelled ceiling, when the image had been set in careful balance directly beneath it and drew the iron to itself by natural force, the image should seem to the people to have risen up and to hang in the air. And so that this should not be betrayed by its quick fall, the ministers of the deception used to say: 'The Sun has risen, so that he may bid farewell to Serapis and depart to his own place.' But many other things too had been built in the place by the men of old for the sake of deception, which it would take too long to list one by one now. But, as we had begun to say, when the rescript had been read out, the crowds of our people were ready to overthrow the author of the error; yet a certain belief had been spread abroad by the pagans themselves, that if a human hand touched that image, the earth would gape open and at once dissolve into chaos, and the sky would suddenly come crashing down. This produced a kind of paralysis in the crowds for a little while. When, behold, one of the soldiers, armed more with faith than with weapons, seized a double axe and, rising up with all his strength, struck the old trickster's jaw. A shout goes up from both peoples; and yet neither did the sky fall nor the earth sink. Then, striking again and again, he hacks at the smoke-blackened godling of rotten wood; when it was thrown down and fire put to it, it burned up as easily as dry wood. After this the head is wrenched from the neck, the corn-measure pulled down, and it is dragged off; then the feet and other limbs, hewn with axes and hauled with ropes, are torn apart, and limb by limb, in place after place, in the sight of Alexandria his worshipper, the decrepit old man is burned. Finally the trunk that was left is burned up in the amphitheatre; and this was the end of Serapis, of empty superstition and ancient error. About his origin the pagans hold differing opinions. Some think him Jupiter, on whose head the corn-measure was placed either because it shows that he governs all things with measure and limit, or that life is supplied to mortals by the abundance of crops. Others think him the power of the river Nile, by whose wealth and fertility Egypt is fed. Some say the image was fashioned in honour of our Joseph, [and of] the measuring out of grain by which he came to the aid of the Egyptians in a time of famine. Others say it is found in the ancient histories of the Greeks that a certain Apis, a householder or a king established at Memphis in Egypt, when grain had run short at Alexandria in a time of famine, supplied the citizens with food in abundance from his own stores; that when he died, they set up a temple to him at Memphis, in which an ox is kept as a token of the excellent farmer, having certain marks of colour, and is called Apis after his name; and that they brought to Alexandria the *soros*, that is, the coffin, in which his body lay, and named it first, by joining Soros Apis, 'Sorapis', and later by corruption 'Serapis'. Whether this is true or nothing at all, God will see to these matters. But let us return to what we began.

fixed.before: When she had said this, Calasiris explained everything to Charicleia and, taking her with him, moved away. After going a little way beyond the bodies lying there, they came upon a low mound. There he lay down, putting the quiver under his head, while Charicleia sat, using the bag as a seat. The moon was just rising and lighting up everything with a bright light (for it happened to be the third day after the full moon); and Calasiris, being an old man in any case and worn out by the journey, was overcome by sleep, but Charicleia, kept awake by the cares that beset her, became the spectator of a scene that was unholy, though customary among Egyptian women. For the old woman, thinking she had got a time free of disturbance and unobserved, first dug a pit, and then lit a pyre on one side of it. Laying out the body of her son between the two, she took up an earthenware bowl from a tripod standing nearby and poured honey into the pit, then milk from another, and from a third she poured a libation of wine. Then she took a cake of dough moulded in the likeness of a man, crowned it with laurel and fennel, and threw it into the pit. After all this she took up a sword and, whirling herself into a frenzy of possession, prayed at length to the moon with barbarous names strange to the ear; then she gashed her arm, wiped off some of the blood with a sprig of laurel, and sprinkled it on the pyre. And after performing other prodigies besides, she bent over her son's corpse and, chanting something into his ear, roused him and by her sorcery forced him to stand upright. Charicleia, who had not watched even the first part without fear, now shuddered, and terrified by these unaccustomed happenings she woke Calasiris and made him a spectator of what was being done. Being in the dark, they themselves were not seen, but they could more easily watch what went on in the light by the pyre, and since they were not far off they could hear what was said, for the old woman was now questioning the corpse in a louder voice. Her question was whether his brother, her surviving son, would come back home safe. He answered nothing, but only nodded, ambiguously letting his mother hope for what she wished; then he suddenly collapsed and lay face down. She turned the body over on its back and would not give up her questioning, but with more violent compulsions, as it seemed, chanting much into his ears again, and leaping sword in hand now to the pyre, now to the pit, she roused him once more, and when he stood up she questioned him on the same matters, forcing him to make the prophecy clear not by nods alone but by voice as well.
